claims.text: GPT-4 achieves the highest average response consistency score across character, word, and sentence-level perturbations compared to other foundation models.
GPT-4-Turbo demonstrates a lower average consistency score under query perturbations than GPT-4.
Gemini-1.5-Flash achieves higher consistency scores under perturbation than Gemini-1.5-Pro.
Proprietary language models outperform open-source models (Gemma2-9B and Llama3-8B) on average response consistency under perturbation.
Evaluating models using multi-level query perturbations alters relative robustness rankings compared to semantically similar query testing used in SelfCheckGPT.
GPT-4 under sentence-level perturbations achieves higher average consistency than other evaluated models under character-level perturbations.

evidence.description: Experiments aggregated across English datasets in LongBench show GPT-4 attaining top consistency scores across character, word, and sentence perturbations.
Empirical measurements show GPT-4-Turbo obtaining the lowest average consistency score among proprietary models evaluated.
Performance plots demonstrate Gemini-1.5-Flash exceeding Gemini-1.5-Pro in consistency across evaluated perturbation types.
Gemma2-9B and Llama3-8B scored lower overall consistency scores than all tested proprietary models across all perturbation levels.
GPT-3.5-Turbo placed second under SelfCheckGPT evaluation but dropped to fourth under the proposed perturbation framework, moving behind Gemini-1.5 models.
Direct comparison shows GPT-4's average consistency score under sentence-level noise exceeds the character-level noise scores of all other evaluated models.

methodologies.name: Perturbation-based hallucination evaluation framework
methodologies.description: Measures post-deployment hallucination by applying character, word, and sentence-level perturbations to user queries and computing pairwise consistency scores between original and perturbed responses.

limitations.text: Detecting model hallucinations post-deployment is challenging due to the absence of context or reference standard responses.
Existing RAG evaluation metrics depend on available context and cannot be directly applied to non-retrieval post-deployment settings.
Experimental evaluation was limited exclusively to English language tasks from the benchmark dataset.
